The Toltec cotton rat (Sigmodon toltecus) exhibits a basal metabolic rate measured at 212.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 212.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under standard laboratory conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value that aligns closely with predictions for a rodent of its somatic mass. This relatively elevated resting metabolism likely reflects the high energetic demands of maintaining homeothermy in the warm, humid lowland habitats this species occupies across Mesoamerica. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this metabolic intensity is sustained by a diet dominated by green plant material, which requires substantial gut processing and nutrient extraction. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, resting adults during their inactive phase, ensuring the recorded oxygen consumption reflects true basal conditions. This metabolic trait has direct implications for the species' daily energy budget, influencing foraging time, habitat selection, and ultimately, the pace of life history events.

The maximum body mass attained by reproductively mature females of S. toltecus reaches approximately 100 grams [Wwi = approximately 100 grams], though field surveys indicate substantial individual variation within a range of 70 to 133 grams. This ultimate wet weight places the species among the medium-sized members of the genus, with males typically averaging slightly larger than females in most populations studied. Neonates emerge at a markedly smaller scale, with newborn pups weighing approximately 6.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 6.2 grams] at parturition, a value derived from measurements of captive Sigmodon hispidus considered representative for the congener. This nearly sixteen-fold increase from birth mass to adult size necessitates a prolonged period of intense maternal investment, during which altricial young depend entirely on lactation for their nutritional and thermoregulatory needs.

Under conditions approximating their thermoneutral zone at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], female Toltec cotton rats experience a gestation period lasting 27 days [tg = 27 days]. This relatively brief intrauterine development is characteristic of small-bodied muroid rodents and results in the delivery of altricial young that require extensive post-natal care. Litter sizes typically range from two to seven pups [N_R_i = Litter sizes typically range from two to seven pups] per parturition event, and females produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], a modest reproductive frequency compared to some temperate-zone congeners. This low annual fecundity is counterbalanced by the substantial maternal investment per offspring, likely contributing to high juvenile survival rates in the stable, seasonally predictable environments these rats inhabit.

Developmental milestones in S. toltecus proceed rapidly after birth. Weaning, marking the cessation of lactation and the transition to an independent diet of solid plant material, occurs at 15 days since birth [tx = 15 days since birth] when young are reared at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This abbreviated suckling period reflects the relatively fast growth rates permitted by the nutrient-rich milk of the mother. Following weaning, juvenile animals enter a period of accelerated somatic growth, achieving 40 days since birth at puberty [tp = 40 days since birth at puberty] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This early onset of reproductive maturation ensures that individuals can contribute to the next generation within a relatively brief adult lifespan, a life history strategy well suited to environments with high extrinsic mortality rates.

Longevity records for the Toltec cotton rat, based on extrapolation from the closely related Sigmodon hispidus, indicate a maximum lifespan of 5.2 years [am = 5.2 years] when individuals are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively short potential lifespan is typical for small rodents exhibiting a fast pace of life, characterized by early maturation, high metabolic rates, and intense but brief reproductive effort. Field observations suggest that few individuals in natural populations reach this upper boundary; predation and seasonal resource fluctuations impose substantial mortality, particularly on sub-adults during their first dry season. The combination of a 5.2-year maximum longevity, a 27-day gestation, and a single annual litter producing 2 to 7 pups defines a demographic strategy that balances high juvenile vulnerability against the necessity of population maintenance in dynamic grassland and edge habitats.
